title: Hilbert's 14th Problem: Non-Reductive Groups and the Grosshans Criterion
content: The module docstring frames the core question of Hilbert's 14th problem in the non-reductive case: for which non-reductive algebraic groups G is the invariant ring R^G always finitely generated? For reductive groups, the answer is always YES (Hilbert-Mumford-Haboush). For non-reductive groups, finite generation depends on both the group and its action. The deepest known characterization is Grosshans's theorem (1997): for a closed subgroup H of a reductive group G, k[V]^H is finitely generated for ALL G-representations V iff k[G/H] is finitely generated (i.e., H is a 'Grosshans subgroup'). The classification table shows: finite groups always give fg invariants (Reynolds averaging); G_a acting on ≤3 variables always gives fg (Weitzenböck-Seshadri); G_a^n (n≥13) sometimes doesn't (Nagata's counterexample). Formalization status: infrastructure (InvariantSubset, ReynoldsOperator, invariantSubring) is proved with 0 sorries; Grosshans characterization and observable subgroup criterion are axiomatized due to missing AlgebraicGroup/GITQuotient Mathlib infrastructure.
mathContext: Grosshans (1997): $H \leq G$ reductive closed $\Rightarrow$ ($k[V]^H$ f.g. for all $G$-reps $V$) $\iff$ $k[G/H]$ f.g. (i.e., $G/H$ is quasi-affine). Key examples: $G_a = (k,+)$ (1-dim unipotent) has f.g. invariants for $n \leq 3$ variables (Weitzenböck 1932, Seshadri 1962) but not always for $n \geq 4$ (Daigle-Freudenburg 1999, $n=4$) or $n \geq 14$ (Nagata 1959, explicit counterexample).

title: Invariant Subset and Basic Membership Lemmas
content: `InvariantSubset G R` is the set {r ∈ R | ∀ g, g • r = r} — elements unchanged by every group element. Two immediately proved lemmas: `mem_invariant_zero` (0 is invariant, using `smul_zero g`) and `mem_invariant_one` (1 is invariant, if the action preserves 1). These use Mathlib's `SMulZeroClass` typeclass for the zero case. The Reynolds operator (defined next) is then a linear retraction onto this set. The docstring for `ReynoldsOperator` (lines 86-93) explains the key conceptual point: reductive groups always have Reynolds operators (via Haar measure averaging), while non-reductive groups generally do not — which is the root cause of finite generation failures.
mathContext: $R^G = \{r \in R : g \cdot r = r \; \forall g \in G\}$. A Reynolds operator $\rho : R \to R^G$ is a linear retraction satisfying $\rho(sr) = s\rho(r)$ for $s \in R^G$ (the key module-over-$R^G$ condition). For $G$ reductive in characteristic 0: $\rho(f) = \int_G g \cdot f \, dg$ (Haar measure average). Non-reductive groups (like $G_a$) have no Haar measure in this sense.

title: ReynoldsOperator: Axioms for a Linear Retraction onto Invariants
content: The `ReynoldsOperator` structure axiomatizes the key properties needed for Hilbert's finiteness theorem. It has five fields: `proj` (the retraction map), `proj_invariant` (identity on R^G), `proj_mem` (maps into R^G), `proj_add` (additivity), and `proj_mul_inv` (commutes with multiplication by invariants: ρ(s·r) = s·ρ(r) for s ∈ R^G). The last axiom is the crucial algebraic property: it makes R^G-modules from R-modules. This is why Reynolds operators imply Hilbert's theorem: if R is a finitely generated G-algebra over R^G with a Reynolds operator, then R^G is also finitely generated (as a direct summand argument).
mathContext: Reynolds operator $\rho : R \to R^G$ satisfies: (i) $\rho|_{R^G} = \text{id}$; (ii) $\text{im}(\rho) \subseteq R^G$; (iii) $\rho$ is additive; (iv) $\rho(s \cdot r) = s \cdot \rho(r)$ for $s \in R^G$. Axiom (iv) makes $\rho$ an $R^G$-module map. Hilbert's theorem: if $R^G$ has a Reynolds operator and $R$ is Noetherian, then $R^G$ is f.g. over $k$.

title: Reynolds Operator is Idempotent
content: `reynolds_idempotent` proves ρ(ρ(r)) = ρ(r): the composition ρ ∘ ρ = ρ. This follows immediately from `proj_invariant`: ρ(r) ∈ R^G, so ρ fixes it. The proof is one line: `ρ.proj_invariant _ (ρ.proj_mem r)`. Idempotency characterizes projections algebraically — it confirms that R^G is a retract of R.
mathContext: $\rho^2 = \rho$ follows from $\text{im}(\rho) = R^G$ and $\rho|_{R^G} = \text{id}$. In category theory, $\rho$ is a split epimorphism $R \twoheadrightarrow R^G$ and $R^G \hookrightarrow R$ is a split monomorphism.

title: Invariant Subring and Finite-Group Reynolds Sum Setup
content: `invariantSubring` (lines 127-134) proves that R^G forms a subring of R when G acts by ring automorphisms: the carrier is InvariantSubset G R, and closure under +, ·, neg, 0, 1 is verified using `smul_add`, `smul_mul'`, `smul_neg`, `smul_zero`, `smul_one` from `DistribMulAction` and `MulDistribMulAction`. PART I-C (lines 136-154) opens a section for finite groups: the variables G (finite group) and R (commutative ring with DistribMulAction + MulDistribMulAction) are fixed. The `reynoldsSum` (defined at line 155) will be Σ_{g ∈ G} g•r — this section header sets up the context for the averaged Reynolds operator construction.
mathContext: For $G$ acting by ring automorphisms: $R^G$ is a subring because $g \cdot (r + s) = g \cdot r + g \cdot s$ and $g \cdot (rs) = (g \cdot r)(g \cdot s)$. The Noether averaging for finite groups: if $|G|$ is invertible in $R$, then $\rho(f) = (1/|G|) \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot f$ is a Reynolds operator.

title: Reynolds Sum: Group-Orbit Average
content: The unnormalized Reynolds operator for finite groups: `reynoldsSum r = Σ_{g : G} g • r`, the sum of all group translates. Dividing by |G| (when invertible in R) gives the actual Reynolds operator. This is `noncomputable` because summing over a Fintype is not generally decidable. The Reynolds sum is the canonical way to project any element of R to something G-invariant.
mathContext: $\text{reynoldsSum}(r) = \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot r \in R$. When $|G|$ is invertible in $R$: $\rho(r) = (1/|G|) \cdot \text{reynoldsSum}(r)$ is a Reynolds operator.

title: Reynolds Sum Maps into Invariants
content: `reynoldsSum_mem_invariant` proves that the Reynolds sum is G-invariant: a • (Σ_g g•r) = Σ_g g•r for all a ∈ G. The proof uses `Equiv.sum_comp (Equiv.mulLeft a)`: left multiplication by a is a bijection on G, so Σ_{g∈G} (ag)•r = Σ_{g∈G} g•r. In Lean: `rw [Finset.smul_sum]; simp_rw [← mul_smul]; exact Equiv.sum_comp ...`. This is the key property justifying the Reynolds sum as a projection onto R^G.
mathContext: For $a \in G$: $a \cdot \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot r = \sum_{g \in G} (ag) \cdot r = \sum_{g' \in G} g' \cdot r$ (substituting $g' = ag$, using that left-multiplication is bijective on $G$). This is the orbit-sum invariance — a discrete version of Haar measure invariance.

title: Reynolds Sum: Additivity, Retraction, Zero, Neg, and Multiplicativity
content: Five theorems completing the Reynolds sum infrastructure: `reynoldsSum_add` (additivity from `smul_add` + `Finset.sum_add_distrib`); `reynoldsSum_on_invariant` (on invariant r: reynoldsSum(r) = |G|·r, since g•r = r for all g, so Σ_g g•r = Σ_g r = |G|·r); `reynoldsSum_zero` (= 0 via `smul_zero`); `reynoldsSum_neg` (= -reynoldsSum(r) via `Finset.sum_neg_distrib`); `reynoldsSum_mul_invariant` (if s ∈ R^G: reynoldsSum(s·r) = s·reynoldsSum(r), from `smul_mul'` + `Finset.mul_sum`). Together these confirm the Reynolds sum is additive and commutes with R^G-multiplication — the axioms of a Reynolds operator (up to normalization by |G|).
mathContext: Key: $\text{rS}(sr) = s \cdot \text{rS}(r)$ for $s \in R^G$ because $g \cdot (sr) = (g \cdot s)(g \cdot r) = s(g \cdot r)$ (using $s$ invariant). Also: $\text{rS}(r)|_{r \in R^G} = |G| \cdot r$. If $|G|$ invertible: $(1/|G|) \cdot \text{rS}$ is the true Reynolds operator.

title: GrosshansSubgroup Typeclass and Grosshans's Characterization Theorem
content: PART II: `GrosshansSubgroup G H` is a typeclass with a single field `quotient_fg : True` (placeholder for the actual condition that k[G]^H is finitely generated — this requires AlgebraicGroup infrastructure not yet in Mathlib). The docstring (lines 207-218) explains: H is Grosshans in G if the coordinate ring k[G/H] is finitely generated as a k-algebra, equivalently G/H is quasi-affine. `grosshans_characterization` (lines 223-242) is Grosshans's 1997 theorem: for a reductive G and closed H ≤ G, k[V]^H is f.g. for all G-representations V iff H is Grosshans. The proof direction 'Grosshans ⟹ fg invariants' uses transfer (embedding k[V]^H into k[G×^H V]) plus Hilbert's theorem for the reductive quotient. Due to missing AlgebraicGroup infrastructure, both the class and theorem are axiomatized via `True`.
mathContext: Grosshans (1997): $H \leq G$ reductive closed subgroup. TFAE: (1) $H$ is Grosshans (i.e., $k[G]^H$ is f.g.); (2) $k[V]^H$ is f.g. for ALL $G$-representations $V$; (3) $G/H$ is quasi-affine (i.e., $G/H \hookrightarrow \overline{G/H}$ open with $\overline{G/H}$ affine). Reference: Grosshans, *Algebraic Homogeneous Spaces and Invariant Theory*, Springer LNM 1673 (1997).

title: Finite Groups and Tori are Grosshans Subgroups
content: `finite_group_grosshans` (lines 248-258): any finite subgroup H of a group G is a Grosshans subgroup (proved trivially as `⟨trivial⟩` since the class has placeholder field). The mathematical content in the docstring: k[G]^H ≅ k[G/H] has finitely many cosets, so it is finitely generated; in char 0, finite groups also have Reynolds operators (averaging by 1/|H|). The `reductive_subgroup_grosshans` (lines 260-271) states that reductive subgroups are Grosshans (also trivially proved, needs actual ReductiveGroup hypothesis).
mathContext: Finite $H \leq G$: $|G/H|$ is finite (= $|G|/|H|$ for finite $G$), so $k[G/H] = k^{|G/H|}$ is f.g. In characteristic 0: Reynolds operator is $\rho(f) = (1/|H|) \sum_{h \in H} h \cdot f$. For reductive $H \leq G$ reductive: $k[V]^H$ is always f.g. by Hilbert-Mumford-Haboush applied to $H$.

title: G_a Case, Part IV Summary, and the Absence of Group-Theoretic Characterization
content: Lines 259-323 cover the G_a = (k, +) case and the Part IV summary. The G_a docstring (lines 273-286) gives the classification: for G_a acting on k[x₁,...,xₙ], invariants are f.g. for n ≤ 3 (Weitzenböck 1932, Seshadri 1962), not always for n = 4 (Daigle-Freudenburg 1999), and Nagata's counterexample uses G_a^13 ≤ GL_32. Part IV summary (lines 292-321) gives the complete characterization: sufficient conditions for fg invariants (Grosshans subgroup, finite H, G_a on ≤3 vars, H with Reynolds operator), necessary conditions for non-fg (non-reductive H, non-Grosshans, representation 'large enough'), and three open problems. The key conclusion: **there is no purely group-theoretic characterization** — the same non-reductive group can give fg invariants for some representations and non-fg for others. Characterization is representation-dependent (Grosshans's theorem gives the embedding-dependent answer).
mathContext: Nagata's counterexample (1959): $G_a^{13}$ acts on $k^{32}$; the invariant ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_{32}]^{G_a^{13}}$ is NOT finitely generated. Daigle-Freudenburg (1999): 4-variable counterexample for $G_a$-action. Weitzenböck (1932): $G_a$ acting on $k[V]$ with $\dim V \leq 3$ always gives f.g. invariants. Open: does a purely group-theoretic criterion exist? Is the Grosshans condition decidable for unipotent groups?
